From Particle Masses to Shared Geometry — The Case for Investigating IDWT

Updated November 5, 2026

conditional research

Could the same spatial structure help explain both a particle's mass and what kind of particle it is?

IDWT began when the author asked an earlier GPT to examine particle frequencies as audio data and look for harmonics, without supplying spatial geometries or dimensionalities. The resulting mass pattern led to a simple counting rule that organizes particles into families associated with particular numbers of spatial directions. The proposed rule is m=μCm=\mu Cm=μC, with C=(n+d−1d)C=\binom{n+d-1}{d}C=(dn+d−1​): one shared family scale times the number of configurations through a level n at spatial depth d. Following those assignments leads to further mathematical connections: how an entire field pattern responds to rotation, which patterns admit an internal clock, where three-component structures occur, and how familiar electric-charge ratios can arise together. Polarization—the directional character of an oscillation—connects several of these calculations.

The case for investigation is that the same geometric organization keeps becoming useful in different calculations. Some results single out particular dimensions. Others show how several particle properties can coexist without choosing each one separately. Their strongest connections are explicit equations and combined constructions that another researcher can reproduce.

A recent example makes this approach concrete. The orientation of an existing spin-carrying field profile determines its circulating current. When a field's orientation varies through six normal directions, that orientation, with a reference orientation and the existing determinant branch, gives a spatial charge distribution with the familiar relative charge values, unchanged by a broad class of radial shape changes. This gives a concrete way for charge identity and variable shape to coexist. It re-expresses the existing charge rule rather than deriving it anew. It remains a conditional construction. Whether the occupied particle patterns supply the required orientation variation remains open; section 9.5 gives the equations and review scope.

The proposed physical setting is one field in ten ordinary spatial dimensions plus time. A particle is a pattern of that field; its depth is the number of spatial directions involved in its bound structure. These are physical directions, of the same kind as familiar length, width and height. They are not extra component labels or separate spaces. This is the setting being tested, not an observed dimensionality established by the mass pattern.

The remaining decisive question is whether one consistent field equation can sustain these patterns and select the masses and properties together. Candidate equations now realize some of these requirements together, but a common law selecting the observed spectrum and all the property constructions has not been completed.

1. A Frequency Search That Led to Geometry

The investigation began with a signal-analysis question. According to the author's account, an earlier GPT was asked to examine the Standard Model particle frequencies as though they were audio data and look for harmonics. The prompt supplied neither particle geometries nor spatial dimensionalities. The subsequent dimensional assignments emerged from investigating the frequency relationships. This is the discovery history supplied by the author; an exact reconstruction of the original model's search procedure is not required to reproduce the mathematical relationships developed afterward.

Mass can be expressed in equivalent frequency units, so the search can be reproduced as a mass comparison. Its central rule is:

Particle mass = a shared family scale × a whole-number geometric count.

In symbols, the proposed rule is m=μ(n+d−1d)m=\mu\binom{n+d-1}{d}m=μ(dn+d−1​): d is the number of spatial directions involved in the particle pattern, n is a positive whole-number level, and μ\muμ is the shared mass-equivalent fundamental for that kind of pattern. The binomial coefficient counts all nonnegative d-tuples with total at most n − 1. It is an exact counting identity; interpreting that count as the frequency multiplier is the physical hypothesis. The following sections explain the count and scale prescription before testing the geometry's further consequences.

The count comes from a fixed combinatorial rule, derived in section 3, rather than a separate arbitrary multiplier for each particle. A later conditional shape-energy calculation also selects completed simplex supports whose counts fall on those same rungs; section 3.4 explains the selection and the supplied physical premises. Two integers enter: the depth d and a level n. Changing depth changes the spacing of the allowed counts. A shared scale moves an entire family's predictions together; it cannot adjust each member independently.

The electron and muon illustrate that restriction. Their assigned counts give the exact ratio 3515/17, close to their measured mass ratio. At the muon's assigned level, the next allowed count is more than 17 percent larger. The agreement therefore occurs on a ladder with substantial gaps, not a continuously adjustable sequence. Section 5 compares alternative depths and levels under the declared shared-scale rules. The numerical scale prescription uses the electron as its sole measured dimensional anchor, together with proposed coefficients and reference counts. Those coefficients were developed with the masses known; their origin remains a dynamical question.

The resulting assignments are depth two for W, Z and Higgs; three for down and strange; four for up, charm and top; five for the neutrino mass states; six for electron and muon; and ten for tau. Bottom remains unresolved, and the neutrino absolute scale requires separate treatment. The proposed photon pattern also uses two bound directions, but its zero rest mass does not determine that plane.

The next question is what happens when these same depths enter calculations of other properties. Spin describes how a particle's field pattern transforms under rotation. Color names the three-component transformation structure associated with quarks, not a visible color. Electric charge distinguishes neutral, charged-lepton and fractionally charged quark patterns. The following map previews the results; the linked sections explain their mathematical tools before using them.

1.1 How Results Are Classified

An exact result follows from the stated definitions and mathematical hypotheses, with a derivation given below. A conditional physical construction supplies a field, action or interpretation and derives its consequences; its additional physical premises remain visible. An empirical calibration fixes an input using observations. A proposed interpretation connects mathematics to a physical property without yet deriving all its observed behavior. An open problem is an implication the current mathematics has not established.

These categories can occur within one calculation. For example, the three-channel counting result is exact, the decision to use that complete channel as a physical source is a premise, and reproducing the observed strong interaction from it remains open. This does not make the rank mathematical result uncertain; it specifies its contribution.

The mass comparisons are also stated at their actual accuracy. They are not all within experimental uncertainty: section 4 gives every numerical output, including the approximately 2.20 percent top discrepancy. The very small reference-distribution coverages in section 5.3 quantify a declared retrospective mass-and-ratio test. They are not odds that the whole theory is true, and the geometric results are not multiplied into them as additional probability factors.

1.2 Why Shared Assumptions Strengthen the Research Case

A geometric premise becomes more useful when it does several jobs successfully. If choosing a structure yields a charge fraction, fixes how its color components transform and remains compatible with its spin and clock, those are multiple consequences of one choice. The shared premise is then a concrete point at which the construction can succeed or fail together; the consequences deserve to be examined jointly.

Several combinations have already been checked explicitly. A spin doublet and an independent color triplet retain a compatible clock while restricting its allowed form. The charge construction changes the relative charge of two triplets without changing their color transformation type. A spatially differentiated charge operator preserves the displayed charge labels and commutes with observer spin for the stated free equation. A same-field contact combines spatial chirality and independent color while retaining the full field needed for spatial derivatives. The newer curvature construction also connects the spinor's orientation and circulation to the existing charge rule, and calculates how that charge can survive radial shape changes; this addition remains pending independent review. Section 13 collects these compatibility checks and lists every additional premise.

This is where the case goes beyond a list of matching numbers: it contains calculations of what happens when useful ingredients are put together. It also records combinations that remain unfinished. In particular, the smallest component system used by the clock selector is not automatically the full field used by the spatial equation. The proposed free charge must survive interactions, and separate localization equations have not yet been joined to all the property constructions. These are specific mathematical tasks for a common theory.

Shared assumptions can provide explanatory economy without establishing a numerical chance estimate. Statistical independence or dependence of empirical tests requires a stated joint model; it cannot be decided simply by counting the formulas or noticing that they share a premise.

1.3 An Invitation to Reproduce and Extend the Work

The central research request is to determine whether these pieces can be realized by one physical field equation. That means sustaining spatial patterns, selecting their occupied counts and common-frequency oscillation, and preserving the required spin, charge and color response when patterns interact. A successful construction should explain several of these features with the same choices and normalization. A demonstrated incompatibility would identify which choice must be repaired or replaced.

A reader can enter at several levels. Sections 3–5 give the count rule, scale inputs and reproducible mass comparisons. Sections 6–10 develop the geometric property calculations. Section 13 is the shortest route to their shared assumptions and tested compatibility; section 14 states the unfinished target. The reproduction appendix and glossary/index support checking the details.

The invitation is to test a connected mathematical programme: reproduce its strongest results, challenge the added premises, and develop the common dynamics where the calculations already meet.

2. Physical Setting, Data and Notation

2.1 One Physical Spacetime

A field assigns component values to each physical position and time. A component is one number needed to describe that field locally; it is not an additional coordinate in which a particle moves. We write a spatial point as x=(x1,…,x10)x=(x_1,\ldots,x_{10})x=(x1​,…,x10​) and time as ttt. A formula on Rd\mathbb R^dRd below may describe a pattern's dependence on only ddd of those spatial directions. Its extension through the remaining directions must still be specified before it is a complete ten-dimensional field configuration.

For example, z=a+ibz=a+ibz=a+ib can record two real components aaa and bbb. Multiplication by iii rotates that pair to (−b,a)(-b,a)(−b,a); it does not create a complex physical dimension. Where pairs of spatial axes are grouped in the same notation, both axes remain ordinary real directions in the same space.

The physical setting is ten ordinary spatial dimensions plus time. All spatial directions are of the same physical kind. A pattern's depth d describes its dimensional involvement within that shared space. It does not introduce a second space, an internal physical dimension, a compactified direction or a separate manifold for each particle family.

Complex coordinates below encode pairs of real field components or paired ordinary spatial directions. Later algebraic constructions and finite lists of coefficients are mathematical descriptions of the field; they are not additional places in which physical events occur. Every field equation must ultimately act on the single physical field, Psi_infinity, on this spacetime.

A localized pattern is concentrated near a spatial region, possibly with tails that decay rather than end abruptly. Its internal field shape is distinct from the position of the whole pattern. For the electron, the project's existing orbit-plus-precession picture concerns literal motion around a nucleus through the surrounding physical space. The proposed trajectory uses four directions within that six-dimensional setting; it does not reduce the electron's own six-dimensional structure to four.

There are no mediator particles in the proposed physical interpretation. Interaction kernels describe responses of the same field. Electrons retain literal deterministic trajectories in their six physical spatial directions. Their internal classical field structure, their external position and time-averaged detector registration are distinct. None of the norms or integrals below postulates a probability cloud or a Born position law.

An eigenvector of an operator retains its direction when the operator acts; the multiplying number is its eigenvalue. A trace adds a matrix's diagonal entries. A determinant measures the signed volume scaling of a linear map; it vanishes when the relevant columns are linearly dependent. For complex entries it also carries phase information, interpreted throughout as algebra of paired real components. An inner product, such as u†vu^\dagger vu†v, measures overlap; zero overlap means orthogonality. Tensor products, written ⊗\otimes⊗, keep two sets of component labels simultaneously. A simplex generalizes a line segment, triangle and tetrahedron to higher dimensions. In this count it is the region of allowed nonnegative exponent labels whose sum is bounded. 3.3 How Equal-Frequency Portions Can Produce a Count Multiplier

A portion is the proposed physical part of a pattern that performs one cycle at the common fundamental. A phase specifies where it is in that cycle. Fixed phase differences mean that portions remain synchronized in frequency, even when they reach a given stage at different times. “Equally splayed” phases are evenly spaced through one full cycle. A Fourier expansion decomposes a waveform mathematically into sinusoidal terms; it does not assert that separate objects oscillate at all those frequencies.

The current portion hypothesis uses C oscillators of the same fundamental within one particle. Fourier terms describe their combined waveform; they are not C independently resonating higher modes.

Let T_0 be the common fundamental period. If each portion contributes one registered event per cycle, additive registration gives

lim⁡T→∞Nevents(T)T=CT0,(3.7) \lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{N_{\rm events}(T)}{T}=\frac C{T_0}, \tag{3.7} T→∞lim​TNevents​(T)​=T0​C​,(3.7)

for fixed phase offsets, including uneven offsets. Counting remains valid without a perfectly uniform external repetition pattern. It presumes that the physical observable registers the events additively.

Equation (3.7) concerns an average event count. Unevenly spaced events can give the same long-time rate without forming a uniform repeating signal. ∑r=0C−1s(x+r/C)=s(Cx).(3.8) \boxed{\sum_{r=0}^{C-1}s(x+r/C)=s(Cx).} \tag{3.8} r=0∑C−1​s(x+r/C)=s(Cx).​(3.8)

To prove it, write the left side as Cx+(C-1)/2 minus sum floor(x+r/C) minus C/2, and use sum floor(x+r/C)=floor(Cx). This gives Cx-floor(Cx)-1/2. The sum has C resets per fundamental period. Equally splayed sinusoids instead sum to zero for C >= 2; the waveform and registration matter.

The identity and event-rate result are exact under their respective definitions. The claim that a sustained field pattern contains exactly S(n,d) such portions, and that its registered rate is its physical mass frequency, is the physical mechanism to establish. Neither the simplex count nor phase locking alone selects an occupied n. Adding one portion changes C by one; it does not prove that the new configuration is sustained.

4. Calculating the Sector Scales

4.1 The Numerical Prescription and Its Inputs

The count law needs a dimensional unit before it produces masses. This section gives the complete numerical recipe used for that unit. A dimensionless coefficient changes a ratio; a dimensional scale carries units such as MeV/c2c^2c2. Here gddg_{dd}gdd​ is the former and μd\mu_dμd​ the latter. The letter ggg is reused for unrelated coefficients in later candidate equations; those equations do not derive this table simply by using the same letter.

The recipe has two levels of input: prescribed numerical coefficients and reference counts, followed by the measured electron mass that sets the overall units. A calibrated or retrospectively proposed recipe can be tested, but its numerical success is distinct from deriving its coefficients from field dynamics.

The non-neutrino numerical prescription uses the dimensionless sector coefficients

g22=14452,g33=87,g44=127,g66=g10,10=14.(4.1) g_{22}=\frac{1445}{2},\quad g_{33}=8\sqrt7,\quad g_{44}=\frac{12}{\sqrt7},\quad g_{66}=g_{10,10}=\frac14. \tag{4.1} g22​=21445​,g33​=87​,g44​=7​12​,g66​=g10,10​=41​.(4.1)

These are prescribed numbers. Their interpretation as physical interaction strengths and their derivation from a master equation remain open. They were developed in attempts to explain previously fitted scales. Using one measured reference to evaluate them is not a historically blind prediction. No discarded particle-index generation rule is needed or asserted here.

The fixed reference counts are

C2⋆=C3⋆=1,C4⋆=15,C6⋆=18564.(4.2) C_2^\star=C_3^\star=1,\quad C_4^\star=15,\quad C_6^\star=18564. \tag{4.2} C2⋆​=C3⋆​=1,C4⋆​=15,C6⋆​=18564.(4.2)

The reference mass Mref,dM_{{\rm ref},d}Mref,d​ is the mass assigned to the chosen reference count Cd⋆C_d^\starCd⋆​. The star here marks a reference entry; it is neither conjugation nor the Hodge star. Equation (4.3) assumes that squared reference masses divided by their sector coefficients share one value. Taking its positive square root gives a reference mass, and dividing by the reference count gives the unit μd\mu_dμd​. Thus the square roots enter through this assumed squared-mass relation.

The common anchor relation and its algebraic consequence are

Mref,d2gdd=me2g66,μd=Mref,dCd⋆=meCd⋆gddg66.(4.3) \frac{M_{{\rm ref},d}^2}{g_{dd}}=\frac{m_e^2}{g_{66}},\qquad \mu_d=\frac{M_{{\rm ref},d}}{C_d^\star} =\frac{m_e}{C_d^\star}\sqrt{\frac{g_{dd}}{g_{66}}}. \tag{4.3} gdd​Mref,d2​​=g66​me2​​,μd​=Cd⋆​Mref,d​​=Cd⋆​me​​g66​gdd​​​.(4.3)

μ10=μ6.(4.5) \mu_{10}=\mu_6. \tag{4.5} μ10​=μ6​.(4.5)

Equal g_10,10 and g_66 do not by themselves prove this equality: the reference normalization or, in a spatial realization, the normalized overlaps must also match. It expresses the shared-pattern-kind premise.

5. How the Spectrum Restricts the Depth Assignments

5.1 Ratios and Fixed-Index Diagnostics

A common scale can move a whole family's mass ladder up or down, but cannot change the ratios of its rungs. This makes within-family ratios useful tests of the depth assignment. Two different searches must be distinguished: this subsection keeps the reported level labels fixed while changing depth; the next permits all positive integer labels while retaining the shared scale rules and complete family assignments.

Within one family the scale cancels:

mimj=S(ni,d)S(nj,d).(5.1) \frac{m_i}{m_j}=\frac{S(n_i,d)}{S(n_j,d)}. \tag{5.1} mj​mi​​=S(nj​,d)S(ni​,d)​.(5.1)

For example,

mμme=383838018564=351517.(5.2) \frac{m_\mu}{m_e}=\frac{3838380}{18564}=\frac{3515}{17}. \tag{5.2} me​mμ​​=185643838380​=173515​.(5.2)

The electron and muon are both high counts of their common fundamental; neither is that fundamental. At the muon label the next count is 17.14 percent higher and the preceding count 15 percent lower. The much smaller archived mass mismatch cannot be removed by moving one rung. Changing mu_6 instead also changes the electron.

The logarithm measures multiplicative discrepancies: being a factor above or below a value is treated symmetrically. In (5.3), rrr is the number of family entries, μ^d\widehat\mu_dμ​d​ is the best common scale for this diagnostic, and ϵd\epsilon_dϵd​ is their root-mean-square logarithmic discrepancy. Optimizing this comparison scale is a diagnostic operation; it does not replace the electron-based prescription of section 4.

A ratio diagnostic can hold the stated indices fixed and optimize a common scale for each trial depth. With benchmark masses M_i and counts C_i(d),

log⁡μ^d=1r∑ilog⁡(Mi/Ci(d)),ϵd2=1r∑i[log⁡μ^dCi(d)Mi]2.(5.3) \log\widehat\mu_d=\frac1r\sum_i\log(M_i/C_i(d)),\qquad \epsilon_d^2=\frac1r\sum_i\left[\log\frac{\widehat\mu_dC_i(d)}{M_i}\right]^2. \tag{5.3} logμ​d​=r1​i∑​log(Mi​/Ci​(d)),ϵd2​=r1​i∑​[logMi​μ​d​Ci​(d)​]2.(5.3)

Scanning integer depths 1 through 15 gives minima at 2 for W/Z/H, 3 for down/strange, 4 for up/charm/top and 6 for electron/muon. Bottom is excluded from the ordinary down/strange ratio diagnostic. The neutrino ratio at its fixed triple favors five; its neighboring-depth values are about 0.05550 at four and 0.01686 at six. The tau comparison

mτ(d)=meS(23,d)S(13,6)(5.4) m_\tau(d)=m_e\frac{S(23,d)}{S(13,6)} \tag{5.4} mτ​(d)=me​S(13,6)S(23,d)​(5.4)

favors ten only with the shared charged-lepton unit retained. A free per-depth tau scale would fit that single mass at every depth.

5.2 A Complete Assignment Theorem with Unrestricted Positive Indices

An exhaustive assignment statement needs a specified set of permitted alternatives. Here a block is a whole particle family, kept together when moved to another depth. “Bijectively” means that each block occupies one of the listed depths and each depth is used once. The proof also keeps the numerical scale recipe. It is therefore stronger than the preceding fixed-index scan, but is not a theorem about every conceivable mass formula.

The proof uses monotonicity: at fixed depth the count increases strictly with positive integer nnn. Once a target is trapped between two neighboring predictions, all other integers are excluded on that side. Fourth powers remove the radicals in the scale ratios, allowing the decisive inequalities to be checked with exact rational numbers rather than rounding-dependent comparisons.

A stronger test moves the intact blocks (WZH, dsb, uct, e-mu, tau) bijectively among {2,3,4,6,10}. It retains the scale prescription, the exact electron reference and the common electron/tau unit, and permits every particle any positive integer index. It is not an arbitrary finite scan.

Put a_d = mu_d/m_e. Their fourth powers are rational:

a24=28902,a34=7168,a44=25639375,a64=a104=1185644.(5.5) a_2^4=2890^2,\quad a_3^4=7168,\quad a_4^4=\frac{256}{39375},\quad a_6^4=a_{10}^4=\frac1{18564^4}. \tag{5.5} a24​=28902,a34​=7168,a44​=39375256​,a64​=a104​=1856441​.(5.5)

The electron equation a_d S(n,d)=1 excludes depths two and three because their first rungs exceed one. At four, one lies strictly between a_4 and 5a_4; at ten, 18564 lies strictly between S(7,10)=8008 and S(8,10)=19448. At six the unique exact solution is S(13,6)=18564. Strict monotonicity covers all other positive indices. Hence electron/muon is at six. Shared unit and distinct depths then put tau at ten.

Only depths two, three and four remain. At three the W benchmark lies between the n = 45 and 46 predictions; their fourth-power ratios are below 81/100 and above 26/25. At four it lies between n = 58 and 59, with fourth-power ratios below 4/5 and above 41/40. These bracket bounds exclude even a 0.5 percent W tolerance at either depth. Thus W/Z/H is at two. The first up-type rung at three exceeds twice the up benchmark, so even a 100 percent tolerance forces that family to four. The remaining down-type block is at three. Every certificate uses the exact archived decimal inputs as rationals, not floating-point accept/reject tests.

A bracket certificate records inequalities that locate the answer, rather than merely reporting the outcome of a search. For nearest logarithmic distance, the boundary between two positive predictions is their geometric mean. Squaring the target therefore gives the neighboring-product inequalities in (5.6). This is why the proof can cover arbitrarily large positive indices without inspecting each one.

At fixed depth, the unique nearest logarithmic rung n_star > 1 is certified by

They certify every maintained comparison index, including n = 17 as the unresolved ordinary bottom control. Doubling an upper index and binary-searching the bracket also finds the nearest rung without an arbitrary index cutoff.

The resulting theorem is conditional: under this scale law, intact blocks, distinct occupied depths and shared lepton reference, the maintained arrangement uniquely matches or improves every individual maintained accuracy. It does not prove uniqueness under every possible scale law, family regrouping or physical theory. It supplies a concrete joint test to combine with the separately derived property constraints.

5.3 Joint Absolute-Mass and Ratio Accuracy

The statistical comparison requires every selected mass to retain its achieved absolute accuracy and every within-family ratio to retain its achieved accuracy. Similar signed mass offsets can cancel in a ratio, so acceptable absolute errors alone do not necessarily preserve that ratio match. These requirements are imposed together on one mass list.

A joint calculation retains both, using the unchanged mass prescription P=m_e a_d C(n,d), C(n,d)=binomial(n+d−1,d), with the coefficients and reference counts given in section 4. The electron is the sole anchor. W, down and up are scored targets, as are Z, Higgs, strange, charm, top, muon and tau. No sector scale is independently fitted. Bottom remains an unresolved ordinary-rung exception; neutrino absolute masses require separate calibration and are not included in this positive-mass test.

All five blocks may move among the specified depths before the exact electron-reference and common-lepton-scale conditions are applied. As established in section 5.2, these equations leave six admissible permutations of WZH, down/strange and up/charm/top over depths two, three and four, with electron/muon at six and tau at ten. The integer search includes every allowed joint tuple, including repeated and non-nearest indices where relevant.

For each nonanchor label, let r_i=log(P_i^*/M_i) be the signed residual of its maintained prediction against the archived central mass. Freeze the actual achieved absolute and ratio bounds

The electron residual is zero. Its ratios with muon and tau duplicate their absolute bounds, while tau/muon supplies a further joint constraint. All pair strips are imposed together; their probabilities are not multiplied as independent evidence.

A looser match still supplies its own constraint. Under the same reference ensemble and allowed search, adding a requirement cannot increase the accepted fraction: the joint accepted set is contained in the set obtained by dropping that requirement. Thus the looser top bound does not relax the tighter muon or boson bounds. Ratio constraints can further reduce the same accepted set; they are not independent extra probability factors.

The bounds use the central residuals themselves, without replacing them by experimental uncertainty floors. For example, the muon absolute log bound is 0.00001730021744; the Z/W ratio bound is 0.0003373485332; and the Higgs/Z ratio bound is 0.00006753194134. Full values, empirical definitions and quoted errors are supplied in the reproducibility packet. This tests achieved central numerical proximity, not a claim that every formula prediction agrees within measurement errors.

For a declared reference ensemble, fix the electron and draw the ten other log mass ratios uniformly from 0 to log R. Sort within WZH, down/strange, up/charm/top and the muon/tau pair. All ten nonanchor masses remain randomized and scored. The resulting density is 144/(log R)^10 on the ordered region. This distribution is an explicit numerical comparison, not a physical law for possible masses.

The acceptance region is too small to estimate efficiently by waiting for ordinary random spectra to pass. Instead, the calculation samples the component acceptance regions directly and corrects their sampling density. For the actual signed-residual ordering, the full set of absolute and ratio constraints is exactly a box in each family's first residual and successive residual differences. Their shared spin, charge and depth results must not be multiplied as independent probability factors. Deriving the coefficient law, selecting and sustaining the occupied counts, resolving bottom and supplying a neutrino absolute scale remain open physical questions.

6. A Spatial Field Pattern with Spin One-Half

The spin result concerns how an entire spatial pattern changes when rotated, including its dependence on position. The explicit profile below carries the half-angle law associated with spin one-half. Whether its squared magnitude integrates to a finite value also gives a useful depth comparison.

6.1 The Profile and Its Equation

A spinor is a set of field components with a specified response to spatial rotations. It differs from an ordinary vector: its rotation rule can change sign after a full 2π2\pi2π turn and return after 4π4\pi4π. That transformation rule is an assumption about the candidate field, not a probability interpretation or a claim that a tiny rigid object literally turns through twice the angle.

The group SO(d)SO(d)SO(d) consists of length- and orientation-preserving rotations of ddd real spatial directions. Its double cover, Spin(d)Spin(d)Spin(d), keeps the extra sign information required for spinors. A representation states how these transformations act on component values. Two descriptions can use different numbers of components while representing the same physical rotation group. No component count changes the number of physical directions.

A Clifford algebra is an algebra of matrices whose products encode the Euclidean inner product. Here its defining rule is γiγj+γjγi=2δijI\gamma_i\gamma_j+\gamma_j\gamma_i=2\delta_{ij}Iγi​γj​+γj​γi​=2δij​I, with δij=1\delta_{ij}=1δij​=1 for equal indices and zero otherwise. It implies that the square of the matrix γ⋅x=∑iγixi\gamma\cdot x=\sum_i\gamma_i x_iγ⋅x=∑i​γi​xi​ is r2Ir^2Ir2I. A Hermitian matrix equals its conjugate transpose. These properties make it possible to combine spatial derivatives and spinor components consistently in the Dirac operator DDD.

The proposed profile below has a radial envelope, which decreases with distance rrr, and a coordinate-dependent spinor factor. The constant unit spinor χ\chiχ is its seed: it specifies the component orientation of the pattern. The parameter aaa controls its spatial scale and AAA its magnitude. This profile is sometimes called a bubble; that term refers to the explicit localized shape, not a material boundary or an extra space.

6.4 Integer-Spin Channels and Photon Polarization

A bilinear expression uses two field factors, for example ξξ†\xi\xi^\daggerξξ†. Its rotation law need not be the same as the law of either factor alone. The Pauli matrices σ1,σ2,σ3\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\sigma_3σ1​,σ2​,σ3​ form a basis for traceless Hermitian two-by-two matrices. Together with the identity they split the bilinear into a scalar part sss, unchanged by rotations, and a vector part vvv, which rotates as an ordinary three-component vector. Their Casimir values distinguish spin zero and spin one.

For light, polarization concerns the directions and relative phases of transverse field components. For a matter particle, spin polarization concerns the orientation of its spin. Connecting either observable to an IDWT spatial field pattern requires its transformation and response laws. Complex coefficients conveniently encode relative phases. Transverse means perpendicular to a specified spatial wave-direction vector KKK. Helicity is the rotation weight about that direction in the observer's three-dimensional description; it is not synonymous with the whole spin representation. The symbol E⊥E^\perpE⊥ denotes directions perpendicular to the plane EEE. These definitions make the photon comparison below precise without replacing the project's photon picture by an exchanged particle.

6.5 Polarization Connections Across the Sectors

Electron spin polarization is measured, for example with the Jefferson Lab Hall A polarimeter. Longitudinal and transverse W/Z polarization is also measured; see the ATLAS joint-polarization result. These observations supply targets for the spatial model, independently of the conventional force interpretation. The maintained assignments put the photon and W/Z at depth two, electron/muon at six and tau at ten. Their familiar observer spin projections number two for the photon, three for massive spin one and two for spin one-half. Depth is therefore not simply the number of measured polarization states.

There are several constructive connections. First, the invariant clock of section 7 commutes with spatial rotations. Rotating a pattern's polarization can leave its fundamental unchanged. The spinor profile (6.1) likewise has the same radial density for every unit seed. Second, the repaired charge operator of section 10 commutes with observer spin: rotating the spin polarization preserves the relative charge eigenvalue. A color triplet and a spin doublet also have commuting actions under their stated independent-color premise. These are useful compatibility conditions for different polarization preparations of the same mass and charge branch.

Third, directional oscillations produce the same kind of oriented spatial two-form that enters the three/four Hodge construction. For a single sinusoidal vector component,

u(t)=acos⁡ω0t+bsin⁡ω0t,Ω=⟨u∧u˙⟩ω0=a∧b. u(t)=a\cos\omega_0t+b\sin\omega_0t, \qquad \Omega=\frac{\langle u\wedge\dot u\rangle}{\omega_0}=a\wedge b. u(t)=acosω0​t+bsinω0​t,Ω=ω0​⟨u∧u˙⟩​=a∧b.

This measures oriented circulation, not yet absolutely normalized angular momentum. One sinusoid traces a plane even in higher dimensions. A spatial texture can have different local planes, and a nonsinusoidal waveform can also combine several planes through harmonics of one common fundamental:

One simple ellipse has zero self-wedge. This connects richer common-frequency polarization to a possible realization of the chiral spatial source in section 8. It does not identify that two-form with independent SU(3) color or replace the existing spinor-bilinear source without a dynamical bridge.

A direct spinor calculation strengthens the spatial connection. With the four-dimensional Clifford convention of the companion note, a positive-chirality seed defines Bij=−iχ†γiγjχB_{ij}=-i\chi^\dagger\gamma_i\gamma_j\chiBij​=−iχ†γi​γj​χ, with zero diagonal. Section 6.6 connects it to the current of the existing spatial profile; its identification with the fundamental temporal waveform remains open. Likewise, the pure-pencil calculation in section 9.3 obtains its four-plus-six reference split by comparing two spinor-derived spatial orientation tensors. Their relative pairings supply a connection between polarization geometry and the charge construction, under that section's full pure-pencil premise.

Finally, average registration of one event per portion per cycle gives C events per cycle regardless of phase offsets, when multiplicity is counted. The oriented circulation depends on those offsets and directions. Thus the proposed mass multiplier can remain fixed while the polarization and reciprocal directional response change. The polarization and sector connections note derives these formulas, gives a same-waveform example and records the finite checks and scoped independent review. A common-field realization joining all these ingredients is still required.

7. A Different Result: Which Minimal Spinors Admit a Clock?

The preceding theorem concerned rotation of a spatial shape. This chapter asks a different question: which minimal component systems permit a rotation-invariant time-evolution term with one time derivative? That kinetic requirement supplies a more selective depth test under its own premises.

7.1 The Invariant Alternating Form

This calculation asks which real component systems can carry a rotation-invariant first-order time term. A module is simply a component space together with the specified action of a group or algebra. “Irreducible” means it cannot be split into smaller nonzero invariant component spaces; “minimal” chooses the smallest spinor system of the stated type. The word fibre, used below, refers to components at a physical point. It is not a separate physical manifold.

The commutant is the set of all linear operations that commute with the prescribed rotations. Real Schur theory says that for this irreducible situation the commuting algebra is real, complex or quaternionic. Those names specify multiplication rules for real matrices: R\mathbb RR, C\mathbb CC and H\mathbb HH. Quaternions have three independent imaginary directions with square minus one. None of these algebras changes real physical spacetime.

A real matrix is skew when JT=−JJ^T=-JJT=−J. It defines an alternating pairing, for which qTJq=0q^TJq=0qTJq=0. In even spatial dimension the spinor rotation representation can split into two chiral branches, distinguished by the sign of an oriented product of Clifford matrices. Choosing one chirality chooses one such branch. This algebraic chirality is defined relative to the stated spatial construction; it is not automatically the observed left- or right-handed interaction behavior of a particle.

Let V be one minimal irreducible real Spin(d) module. Seek a nondegenerate real skew matrix J commuting with every rotation of V. 7.3 The Essential Carrier Qualification

A carrier is the complete set of field components on which the proposed equations act. Restricting which spatial rotations are considered does not automatically remove components from that carrier. This is why a theorem about one minimal spinor cannot be transferred unchanged to a larger field containing several copies. The distinction affects which clocks are allowed, not just how they are named.

A full ambient field restricted to a lower depth need not be minimal. The real 32-dimensional Spin(10) half-spin module restricts with repeated copies; its skew commutant dimensions at seven, eight and nine are 6, 2 and 1. Those copies restore clocks. An even number of real-type copies can pair into an invertible skew form. Second-order dynamics also evade the first-order criterion.

The later massive Clifford field has complex dimension 32, or real dimension 64. Calling that field and the minimal real module the same carrier would be incorrect. A common physical theory would need to isolate the minimal active pattern used in the selector while retaining the full kinetic structure needed by its spatial evolution. This isolation is open.

8. Why the Complete Middle-Hodge Channel Has Three Components at Three/Four

8.1 The Rank Theorem

This chapter uses another way to describe oriented spatial data. A one-form is a linear rule that assigns a number to a tangent vector, such as extracting its component along an axis. A two-form assigns signed values to oriented area elements; higher forms extend this idea to higher-dimensional oriented elements. Their components are antisymmetric: exchanging two directions reverses the sign. The notation ΛmV\Lambda^m VΛmV denotes the degree-mmm exterior forms or equivalent exterior components, using the Euclidean metric to identify the relevant vector and covector descriptions.

The wedge product, ∧\wedge∧, combines such oriented elements antisymmetrically. Repeating a direction gives zero. A basis wedge of independent directions is called a blade. In 2m2m2m directions an mmm-form has middle degree: its complementary oriented element also has mmm directions.

The Hodge star uses the physical Euclidean metric and an orientation to send each oriented element to its perpendicular complement. In three dimensions it relates an oriented area to its normal direction; in four dimensions it sends two-forms to two-forms. Applying it twice gives the sign in (8.1). A Hodge eigenform is a component combination carried into a multiple of itself by that operation. The two eigenspaces are the chiral channels used here. When the eigenvalues are +i+i+i and −i-i−i, the complex notation encodes paired real components; it does not change physical space.

“Complete channel” means that every component in one such eigenspace is retained. “Shadow” means the specified relation between the odd-dimensional data and its containing even-dimensional spatial channel, not a second physical space. This relation is an additional premise. The normal covector n♭n^\flatn♭ in the next paragraph evaluates the component along a chosen unit normal. Its nnn is unrelated to the mass-level index nnn.

8.2 A Spatial Triple Is Not Yet Independent Color

Three components can carry different transformation laws. An ordinary real spatial vector has three entries, but its rotations are SO(3)SO(3)SO(3). A complex color triplet carries the SU(3)SU(3)SU(3) action defined in section 7.4, with eight independent generators. Matching the number three does not identify these groups or supply independent color transport.

Here normal means perpendicular to a selected spatial subspace. A four-base is a chosen four-dimensional subspace within physical ten-space, leaving six perpendicular directions. It is a reference split of the same space, not yet the bound/free split of an identified particle. Three pairs of those six directions can be encoded using C3\mathbb C^3C3. The exterior degrees zero through three have 1,3,3,11,3,3,11,3,3,1 component labels, totaling eight; this explains the factor eight in (8.4).

The operators ai†a_i^\daggerai†​ and aja_jaj​ insert and remove exterior labels algebraically. They are not particle creation and annihilation mechanisms here. Parity of exterior degree means whether that degree is even or odd. A normal Clifford matrix changes that parity, which is why projecting to one fixed degree can erase required normal derivatives.

The infinitesimal generators of a continuous group form its Lie algebra, with commutators recording how small transformations combine. The lowercase notation su(3)\mathfrak{su}(3)su(3), or su(3) in prose, denotes the algebra of SU(3)SU(3)SU(3). Similarly SU(2)SU(2)SU(2) consists of determinant-one unitary two-by-two matrices and supplies the double-cover rotation law for a spin doublet. An algebra of three spatial rotation generators is not an algebra of eight independent color generators.

A real triple of middle-form components rotates as a spatial vector in the three-dimensional shadow. Its rotation algebra has three generators, not eight. If three equivalent complex modes possess independent norm-preserving and volume-preserving transport, their algebra is su(3). That equivalence and transport are physical premises to realize.

9. A Common Geometric Carrier for Relative Electric Charges

9.1 Exterior Degree and a Determinant Branch

A weight records the phase acquired under a specified one-parameter rotation: weight qqq means multiplication by eiqθe^{iq\theta}eiqθ. It is a transformation label, not yet an integrated electric source. Under a common phase rotation of three component labels, a degree-two exterior expression acquires two phases and a degree-three determinant acquires three. The inverse determinant acquires the opposite three phases. These simple addition rules produce the charge table below.

The central U(1)U(1)U(1) of U(3)U(3)U(3) rotates all three entries by the same phase and commutes with every U(3)U(3)U(3) matrix. A character is a one-dimensional representation, so the determinant character records a single phase. In this section D=det⁡WD=\det WD=detW means that determinant representation; it is not the Dirac operator DDD from section 6 or the spatial dimension DDD used later. The symbol 1\mathbf11 denotes a singlet. A direct sum, ⊕\oplus⊕, retains alternative component blocks, while a tensor product combines their labels.

The six real normal directions remain ordinary physical directions. The exterior construction is a way of describing how components associated with those directions transform. It does not establish new independently variable component geometry without a field realization.

Let W encode three complex pairs of ordinary normal spatial directions; its real dimension is six. Write D=det⁡WD=\det WD=detW. On

F=1⊕Λ2W,E=F⊗(1⊕D−1),(9.1) F=\mathbf1\oplus\Lambda^2W,\qquad E=F\otimes(\mathbf1\oplus D^{-1}), \tag{9.1} F=1⊕Λ2W,E=F⊗(1⊕D−1),(9.1)

the central rotation W↦eiθWW\mapsto e^{i\theta}WW↦eiθW has weights 0,2,-3,-1. Their multiplicities are 1,3,1,3. Normalizing the determinant weight three to a unit gives

Because every SU(3)SU(3)SU(3) matrix has determinant one, multiplying a block by the determinant character changes its central U(1)U(1)U(1) phase but leaves its SU(3)SU(3)SU(3) color type unchanged. This explains why the two triplets in the table have the same color type while carrying different relative charges.

The next factorization introduces a local square root of that determinant phase, denoted LLL. “Local” qualifies the choice of phase branch; the original expression (9.1) needs no such square-root choice. The charge table is exact given the carrier and normalization. Assigning its blocks to physical particles at particular depths is an additional identification. It is compatible with singlet charged leptons at six and ten and a neutral five-depth pattern; it does not, alone, force those depths. 9.2 What Can Select the Six Normal Directions?

The charge table used six normal directions as an input. This separate argument asks whether another geometric requirement singles out that number. A bilinear map takes two spinor inputs and returns a vector; alternating means it changes sign on exchanging the inputs and vanishes if they are equal. Spin-equivariant means rotating both inputs rotates the output in the corresponding ordinary vector way.

The strong extra requirement is that every linearly independent pair give a nonzero output. It is stronger than requiring one useful pair. The matrices in (9.2) test whether the desired map exists and has the required exchange sign. Equation (9.3) then compares the number of independent spinor inputs available after fixing one input with the number of possible output components. A map that is injective on those remaining inputs needs at least that many output directions. The complex notation used for this test is algebraic encoding, not a complex physical space.

A conditional independent geometric argument uses a normal chiral spinor S and a Spin-equivariant alternating vector bilinear β:Λ2S⟶NC\beta:\Lambda^2S\longrightarrow N_\mathbb Cβ:Λ2S⟶NC​, with dim⁡N=2m\dim N=2mdimN=2m. 2m−1−1≤2m.(9.3) 2^{m-1}-1\le2m. \tag{9.3} 2m−1−1≤2m.(9.3)

Among the map-bearing dimensions only m=3 satisfies that bound, and Λ2C4≅C6\Lambda^2\mathbb C^4\cong\mathbb C^6Λ2C4≅C6 verifies sufficiency there. A pure spinor is one whose Clifford annihilator has the largest possible isotropic dimension. Its annihilator consists of complex-encoded directions whose Clifford action gives zero on the spinor; isotropic here means zero under the complex-bilinear extension of the spatial quadratic form. Real Euclidean directions themselves do not acquire zero length. Purity is an algebraic condition on the spinor's spatial data. It will be used explicitly in the next construction.

Equivalently, automatic purity of every chiral spinor together with the alternating vector channel selects six. This selects a normal gap under its universal-frame premise; it does not select the gap's endpoints by itself. Selecting only special pairs instead of every independent pair permits higher normal dimensions again.

9.3 A Four-Base Can Be Selected, but the Full Flag Does Not Follow

A pencil here is a two-dimensional linear family of spinors generated by uuu and vvv. A pure pencil requires every nonzero linear combination to be pure; merely requiring both endpoints to be pure is weaker. The notation e12e_{12}e12​ is the exterior product of two basis labels. A decomposable two-form is one that can be written as a single wedge of two vectors, rather than a sum describing several independent planes.

A flag is a nested list of spatial subspaces. Selecting a four-dimensional subspace and its six-dimensional perpendicular complement does not specify every two-, three-, five- and six-dimensional member of a nested list. The question is which of those choices follow from the algebra and which remain extra physical data.

The spinor bilinears JuJ_uJu​ and JvJ_vJv​ below act on real spatial tangent directions. Each encodes a compatible rotation by a right angle in paired planes. Their product distinguishes directions where those pairings agree or oppose; the projectors in (9.4) extract the resulting four-plane and its complement. This uses geometric information of the spinors but does not introduce an additional manifold of orientations.

In the exterior realization of a chiral spatial spinor, an orthogonal pure pencil can be put in the form u=1u=1u=1, v=e12v=e_{12}v=e12​. Every linear combination is pure. Its annihilator data select four ordinary real directions B and their orthogonal complement N. Combined with the preceding six-normal premise this gives B4 plus N6 inside ten-space. The pure-pair stabilizer calculation is related to established mathematics in Krasnov, Geometry of Spin(10) Symmetry Breaking; no gauge-particle interpretation is adopted here.

The stabilizer of given data is the set of transformations that leave it fixed. A chart is a convenient local algebraic parametrization, not an additional physical space. In the exterior chart used next, a pure spinor near the scalar seed 111 is represented by the exterior exponential of a two-form. Requiring the whole pencil to have that form constrains its higher-degree terms, which is the substantive step selecting the four-plane.

The four-plane claim can be reproduced directly. A pure spinor has a maximal isotropic Clifford annihilator; in the exterior chart about 1 it is an exponential of a two-form. Expanding 1+tv=exp⁡B(t)1+tv=\exp B(t)1+tv=expB(t) for every t forces B(t)=tv2B(t)=tv_2B(t)=tv2​, all higher grades of v to vanish, and v2∧v2=0v_2\wedge v_2=0v2​∧v2​=0. Thus v2 is decomposable and can be rotated to e12. For a normalized pure spinor define the actual spatial skew matrix (Jψ)ij=−iψ†γiγjψ(J_\psi)_{ij}=-i\psi^\dagger\gamma_i\gamma_j\psi(Jψ​)ij​=−iψ†γi​γj​ψ off diagonal, with zero diagonal. PB=(I+JuJv)/2,rank⁡RPB=4,PN=(I−JuJv)/2.(9.4) P_B=(I+J_uJ_v)/2,\quad \operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb R}P_B=4, \qquad P_N=(I-J_uJ_v)/2. \tag{9.4} PB​=(I+Ju​Jv​)/2,rankR​PB​=4,PN​=(I−Ju​Jv​)/2.(9.4)

Two pure endpoints alone are insufficient: the whole pencil condition was used. These matrices act on ordinary spatial tangent directions; the algebra does not add a second physical manifold.

The normal six-plane is not the electron's bound six-plane. In coordinates one may take B=⟨e1,…,e4⟩B=\langle e_1,\ldots,e_4\rangleB=⟨e1​,…,e4​⟩, N=⟨e5,…,e10⟩N=\langle e_5,\ldots,e_{10}\rangleN=⟨e5​,…,e10​⟩, but the nested physical six-plane is Q6=⟨e1,…,e6⟩Q_6=\langle e_1,\ldots,e_6\rangleQ6​=⟨e1​,…,e6​⟩. An extra normal complex line is needed to specify it. The normal spinors of this pencil are proportional, so their alternating bilinear is zero: the pencil itself does not provide that extra frame or the entire nested two/three/five/six flag.

Preserving a chosen direction or plane generally leaves fewer rotations available. The subgroup calculation below tests exactly that reduction. It matters because a fixed spatial flag cannot simultaneously be treated as unchanged under every larger normal rotation unless its transformation rule supplies that compatibility.

If normal SU(3) is identified with ambient rotations preserving this fixed Q6, it reduces to U(2); preserving the real Q5 reduces it to SU(2). Full independent color therefore cannot simply mean rotations preserving every fixed bound subspace. A moving compatible embedding or equivalent-mode transport needs its own dynamical construction.

The familiar sixteen-component ambient pure-pair character gives additional conjugate blocks. It is a different carrier from (9.1). Its usual charge generator fails to commute with two observer-spin generators when its two-plane is literal spatial geometry. Matching numerical charge values does not repair that failure. The following differential construction was developed precisely to preserve actual spatial spin and kinetics together.

9.4 A Separate Depth-Five Link between Neutrality and Handedness

This subsection starts a different candidate construction. Its proposed charge is not obtained by restricting the complete table of section 9.1. 10.1 The Angular Repair

The earlier charge tables acted on component labels at a point. A physical spatial equation also differentiates the profile. A label conserved only when those derivatives are omitted is not enough. This chapter adds the coordinate-rotation terms needed to commute with the full free ten-space equation.

The Hamiltonian operator HDH_DHD​ generates time evolution through i∂tψ=HDψi\partial_t\psi=H_D\psii∂t​ψ=HD​ψ. It is first-order in spatial derivatives and has a restoring mass coefficient MMM. Here MMM is a parameter of the candidate equation, not a derived simplex mass. Choosing units ℏ=c=1\hbar=c=1ℏ=c=1 removes conversion constants without changing physical dimensionality. The Hermitian matrix β\betaβ has eigenvalues +1+1+1 and −1-1−1, and its anticommutation with each γi\gamma_iγi​ supplies the usual massive Clifford kinetic structure.

In (10.1), SabS_{ab}Sab​ rotates components, LabL_{ab}Lab​ rotates the spatial arguments in the a,ba,ba,b plane, and JabJ_{ab}Jab​ combines them. A time-independent operator commuting with HDH_DHD​ maps free solutions to solutions and has a conserved integrated expectation under appropriate boundary conditions. The expectation here is a classical field integral, not a statistical probability average.

Use the full complex rank-32 Clifford field on ordinary R10 and set ℏ=c=1\hbar=c=1ℏ=c=1. Let beta anticommute with all ten Hermitian gamma matrices, β2=I\beta^2=Iβ2=I, and define

10.2 What the Repair Has and Has Not Solved

A free equation contains no additional interaction term. A conserved label of that equation must be retested after an interaction is added. It must also have the required behavior under translating a whole isolated pattern: ordinary electric charge should not change because the coordinate origin changes. The next two tests separate these requirements from the already proved free commutator.

This is an exact conserved free-field generator, with suitable decaying domains. It is angular about a selected origin. Higher base angular degree ell changes its spectrum by multiples of ell/3; spin one-half and radial density do not automatically select ell=0. Translations generally fail to commute with this origin-dependent Q. A local interaction also need not preserve it even if ordinary total angular momentum is conserved.

A reciprocal interaction evolves all participating field components through the same action; no profile is merely a fixed external receiver. A centroid is the spatial center defined by the chosen density. Ordinary torque measures the change of total spatial angular momentum. Because QangQ_{\rm ang}Qang​ contains a more particular spin-orbital combination, zero centroid displacement and zero ordinary torque need not make its derivative vanish.

There is a concrete reciprocal counterexample. For the same-field contact V=λρ2/2V=\lambda\rho^2/2V=λρ2/2, take three orthogonal positive-beta Gaussian components of width L centered in a base plane at (b,0),(0,b),(−b,−b)(b,0),(0,b),(-b,-b)(b,0),(0,b),(−b,−b), with polarization signs (1,-1,1). The complete centroid and ordinary total torque vanish, but

d⟨Qang⟩dt=2λb23L2A4(πL22)5[e−b2/L2−e−5b2/(2L2)]>0.(10.5) \frac{d\langle Q_{\rm ang}\rangle}{dt} =\frac{2\lambda b^2}{3L^2}A^4 \left(\frac{\pi L^2}{2}\right)^5 [e^{-b^2/L^2}-e^{-5b^2/(2L^2)}]>0. \tag{10.5} dtd⟨Qang​⟩​=3L22λb2​A4(2πL2​)5[e−b2/L2−e−5b2/(2L2)]>0.(10.5)

Recentring the origin on the centroid cannot cure this example. It is a failure of that particular interaction to conserve the proposed charge, not a theorem against every possible reciprocal same-field interaction.

Another possible repair is to start with a constant component label in a basis where free positive- and negative-energy branches are separated, then transform it back to the original field variables. The Foldy–Wouthuysen map W(p)W(p)W(p) performs that free change of component basis at each momentum ppp. Conjugating an operator means Q0↦WQ0W†Q_0\mapsto WQ_0W^\daggerQ0​↦WQ0​W†. Momentum dependence makes the resulting operation nonlocal in position: its value depends on the spatial profile, not just the components at one point. This is an operator transformation, not a reinterpretation of the electron's physical position.

A translation-invariant comparison conjugates a constant label with the free Foldy-Wouthuysen map

W(p)=Ep+M+(γ⋅p)β2Ep(Ep+M),Ep=p2+M2,Qd=WQ0W†,(10.6) W(p)=\frac{E_p+M+(\gamma\cdot p)\beta}{\sqrt{2E_p(E_p+M)}}, \quad E_p=\sqrt{p^2+M^2},\quad Q_d=WQ_0W^\dagger, \tag{10.6} W(p)=2Ep​(Ep​+M)​Ep​+M+(γ⋅p)β​,Ep​=p2+M2​,Qd​=WQ0​W†,(10.6)

where Q0=(−1)jj/3Q_0=(-1)^j j/3Q0​=(−1)jj/3. It commutes with free H and translations, and its positive-beta weights are 0,-1/3,2/3,-1. However its two triplets are conjugate SU(3) types, not the same type required above. Q_d is nonlocal in position representation, and generic local interactions break it. It is a different comparison, not a simultaneous solution of the charge/color problem.

The physical electric source remains open: a generator, its continuity current, a source law for Psi, reciprocal conservation and a common classical normalization must be demonstrated together. Multiplying a free component weight by an arbitrary field norm does not derive the observed equal charge of the electron, muon and tau.

11. Conjugate Patterns, Magnetic Response and Shape

11.1 An Opposite-Charge Map of the Same Free Equation

A conjugate pattern in this subsection means another exact solution related by a specified transformation. An antiunitary map includes complex conjugation while preserving the norm; in the real encoding it is still a precise operation on real field data. The construction below also reflects one spatial coordinate and reverses the solution's time history. Reversing a history, evaluating the original at −t-t−t, is not the same operation as merely conjugating the field at one fixed time.

The test is whether the transformed history solves the same massive equation and reverses its proposed charge without changing its energy. Passing that test supplies an opposite-label partner. The additional empirical identification with a physical antiparticle is left open.

The angular charge has a same-equation antiunitary construction. Define Be=γ2γ4γ6γ8γ10B_e=\gamma_2\gamma_4\gamma_6\gamma_8\gamma_{10}Be​=γ2​γ4​γ6​γ8​γ10​, P4=βγ4P_4=\beta\gamma_4P4​=βγ4​, A=P4BeA=P_4B_eA=P4​Be​, and let R4 reflect x4. Then

solves the same massive equation, preserves energy and norm, and reverses Qang. This includes higher angular sectors. It survives real nonlinear energies U(sigma)+V(rho), with sigma=psi-dagger beta psi. A bare reflection without the combined map would flip the mass sign, so that omission matters. The exact map is a useful conjugacy result; identifying these two patterns with observed particles and antiparticles, including their interactions, remains a physical interpretation to establish.

Anisotropy means different behavior along different directions. A biradial profile depends on two radii: one in the four-base and one in the six normal directions. It can distinguish those groups while remaining rotationally symmetric within each. Equation (11.7) supplies four coefficient functions, each depending on p,z,tp,z,tp,z,t. The four Clifford factors preserve a closed set of equations for the stated scalar nonlinearities. “Closed” means that substituting this form into the full equation generates only these four factors, so their coefficient equations suffice within the assumed family. It does not mean that the equations already have a sustained localized solution.

The four-plus-six field admits the exact biradial ansatz

11.5 Retained Spin Components Repair a Determinant-Rank Obstruction

A determinant of three copies of one commuting color vector vanishes because its columns are dependent. Retaining the existing two spin columns supplies a possible source of distinct color vectors without appending new fields. The epsilon contractions below use antisymmetry in both color and spin slots. Their component symbols ν,u,e,d\nu,u,e,dν,u,e,d are labels of projected coefficients in this construction; their resemblance to particle names does not establish those identifications.

A subgroup is a subset of transformations closed under the same composition law. Invariance under the listed spin/color subgroup and assigned phase weights is a narrower statement than invariance under the full differential charge operator. The calculation repairs the finite-component contraction only.

are nonzero for commuting components: the two spin columns can supply different color vectors. For example u-up=e1, u-down=e2, d-up=e2, d-down=e3 gives B=(2,0), P=(0,2). Both are color singlets and transform as the corresponding chiral spin doublets. Their tagged charges are qB=0 and qP=1. Hence ν†B\nu^\dagger Bν†B and eTϵPe^T\epsilon PeTϵP are invariant under these subgroup and tagged-charge transformations.

The example shows nonzero algebraic contractions with the stated transformation rules. A positive completion puts a mismatch into a squared norm, such as the difference between an existing component and its proposed nonlinear source. Its expansion contains both coupling and stabilizing square terms, but positivity is not by itself full dynamical stability. A phase-balance vector records how many factors of each component occur, with negative entries for conjugate or oppositely oriented factors. Dotting it with the assigned charge weights tests the corresponding constant-phase invariance.

Positive polynomial completions such as λ∣ν−κB∣2+η∣e−ξϵPˉ∣2\lambda|\nu-\kappa B|^2+\eta|e-\xi\epsilon\bar P|^2λ∣ν−κB∣2+η∣e−ξϵPˉ∣2 use only those same components. Their phase-balance vectors in order (u,d,nu,e) are (1,2,-1,0) and (2,1,0,1), both annihilating q=(2/3,-1/3,0,-1). They break ordinary common phase symmetry, and the neutral contraction also breaks the unmodified normal central circle. Most importantly, subgroup invariance does not prove conservation of the full differential Qang or closure under full ten-space kinetics. This repairs an algebraic rank problem without claiming the interaction bridge has been completed.

12. Localization, Same-Field Tails and Complete Inertia

The algebraic properties do not remove the need for a sustained physical object. This chapter first retains the separate positive second-order and compact-shape constructions. Sections 12.9–12.11 then develop the newer first-order density-law candidate and its same-preparation response and geometry. Results transfer only where the equations and preparation actually agree.

12.1 A Fully Specified Comparison Action

This chapter changes candidate dynamics explicitly. The preceding Clifford equation is first-order and acts on spinor components. The action below is second-order in time and treats its retained components as Lorentz scalars, meaning that their spacetime transformation does not itself carry a spinor index. A derivation connecting the two descriptions has not been supplied. The familiar charge and color labels do not transfer the earlier spin proof to this different action.

A spacetime action integrates a Lagrangian density L\mathcal LL over time and all ten spatial coordinates. Varying it gives coupled field equations. Its kinetic terms contain derivatives and determine inertia and propagation; its potential VVV depends on field values. The signature “plus/minus” means that the squared time derivative enters the contraction with a plus sign and the ten squared spatial derivatives with minus signs. The coefficient Z>0Z>0Z>0 fixes the kinetic normalization.

The component names u,d,s,eu,d,s,eu,d,s,e denote trial projections of the same proposed master field. They are not additional mediator particles. In (12.1), each determinant uses three color vectors evaluated at the same spacetime point, one of which is a derivative. It can therefore be nonzero even though a determinant with two identical columns would vanish. The spacetime index μ\muμ runs over time as well as all ten spatial directions. These determinant vectors Cμ,DμC_\mu,D_\muCμ​,Dμ​ are unrelated to the integer portion count CCC or the Dirac operator DDD.

A numerical solution has two separate tests: whether its discretized equations are solved accurately, and whether those discrete solutions approximate the continuum problem. A residual is the value left when a proposed solution is substituted into the equation; a small residual concerns that equation and its chosen normalization. A grid weights errors differently near an axis, which is why a small weighted residual can conceal a larger pointwise error.

The Hessian is the second variation of the constrained energy. Positive values on a specified set of perturbations mean that energy increases to quadratic order in those directions. Testing only real amplitudes does not test every complex component, shape, singlet or dynamical perturbation. Likewise, being below a dispersal threshold means that spreading into the stated comparison configuration costs more energy; it is not a proof against every decay channel. These distinctions govern the results after the table.

The dispersal threshold is 3. Two finest extrapolations suggest 2.43910. Real-amplitude Hessians were positive on the tested 32,64,96 grids; pure spatial phase changes have exact nonnegative gradient cost. These are restricted tests, not full stability. A weighted optimizer residual hid axis errors; sparse Newton correction on 96/192 grids reduced pointwise discrete residuals below 1e-12 with energy changes below 3.4e-11 per P. Those are discrete equations and convergence estimates, not continuum existence certificates.

The component frequencies are approximately 0.718715 and 0.780906. This is a two-phase relative equilibrium: its shape is stationary while the two component phases advance at their separate rates. It is not yet a particle made of C copies of one fundamental. P is continuous and not selected. No measured mass, physical depth or quantized charge follows from these numerical profiles.

12.5 Stress Balance and Inertia

Localization also requires the directional forces within a pattern to balance. A norm-preserving dilation stretches the profile while reducing its amplitude enough to keep its integrated norm fixed. Applying it separately to the two- and eight-direction groups gives two necessary stationarity conditions. Their difference tests how much directional stress the determinant-gradient term supplies.

The Laue condition states that the integrated spatial stresses vanish for a localized configuration with stationary rest-frame stress, conserved total stress-energy and vanishing surface terms.
