13.2 Explicitly Compatible Choices

The useful question is what happens when the ingredients are actually combined. Does a shared choice preserve both properties, introduce a new constraint, or destroy one of them? The examples below show combinations that have been checked. Their conclusions stay at the algebraic or source-action level where the checks were performed.

First, simplex count and color/spin multiplicity need not compete. On a chosen polynomial band the model spectral label can be μdS(n,d)Ispin⊗Icolor\mu_dS(n,d)I_{\rm spin}\otimes I_{\rm color}μd​S(n,d)Ispin​⊗Icolor​. It is invariant under both actions; a color triplet does not multiply the frequency by three. This is a mathematical compatibility witness, not a derived physical mass operator. If a proposed feedback instead traces over every component, its normalization has to explain why that extra factor is absent.

Second, an independent color triplet and spin doublet coexist while restricting the clock to an ordinary complex direction, as (7.5) proves. The combined assumptions produce a further constraint rather than a contradiction. This is stronger than listing separately compatible ranks.

Third, retaining the full kinetic field and projecting only the bilinear source permits spatial chirality, independent color and a positive three/four contact to coexist in (8.7)–(8.11). The construction gives a single explicit source rule across all assigned depths, with its shadow premise stated. It demonstrates more than coincident terminology.

Fourth, the determinant branch changes normal U(1) charge but leaves SU(3) representation type unchanged. It accounts simultaneously for a charged singlet, a neutral singlet and two equally colored triplets. That is a shared algebraic choice producing several outputs without four independent charge assignments.

Fifth, the actual angular repair combines total spatial spin, both base branches and normal charge on one full kinetic field. The spin and charge operators are not just unrelated matrices attached afterward. Its known interaction defect, however, prevents calling this a finished physical charge theory.

Sixth, one photon two-plane supplies both its two-component polarization description and its circular helicity basis. The two components are not two independently counted portions and supply no extra factor of two in the mass-frequency law. For matter, the invariant clock and the spin-commuting charge generator allow polarization rotation without changing their isolated labels. Section 6.6 now relates the same spinor seed to a circulating norm current with zero integrated transport. Connecting that current to the common-fundamental waveform and the physically normalized Hodge source remains open; the separate quartic contact must not be silently combined with the critical profile equation.

Seventh, section 9.5 connects the circulating spinor profile to a spatial representation of the same charge weights. Its radial deformation family retains those weights while changing size and source moments. This gives a specific compatibility test for localization mechanisms: they can choose a shape without having to change the charge table. The fixed boundary data, reference orientation and determinant branch remain premises, and its transcription has scoped independent review while the action and physical source identification remain open.

Eighth, the adjacent-depth block identity in section 6.7 places an odd-dimensional polarization axis and its neighboring even-dimensional rotation planes in one explicit construction. Its chosen embedding is visible, and it works at both three/four and five/six. This connects existing descriptions without treating the axis as a new particle property or an independent prediction of charge.

Ninth, sections 9.6–9.7 put selected pure-component geometry and reduced charge eigenprofiles into the same candidate density action, using different explicitly stated branches. The exact threshold branch, positive-clock signed-seed branches and full-space radial branch must not be treated as one solution. The full-space branch is the stronger simultaneous example for support, positive momentum response and complete-field circulation (sections 12.9–12.11). Those three results share one preparation; its charge and count selection remain unfinished.

Tenth, sections 9.8 and 12.14 now join the prepared spatial spin doublet, normal singlet/triplet and inherited charge characters to localized moving fields with controlled first-simplex weights under one proposed action. This is an explicit common-law overlap rather than a transfer of conclusions between unrelated equations. Its supplied windows, graph, rank and clock remain visible, and its uniform moving-weight limit has a stated small-momentum regime. Section 9.9 supplies a separate centered-only solution with spatially varying normal geometry and a complete retained normal orbit; that polynomial solution is not asserted to solve the additional-window equation.

The compatible bound/free split now supplies a second depth-by-depth route to the property algebra (sections 9.10–9.12). The same reference six-plane supports the quark pair under both reduced kinetic laws, while the explicit centralizer table exposes the unresolved lepton and boson actions. The corrected massive-carrier comparison (7.5) and six-depth density profiles (12.15) join seed spin and free representation labels to one radial equation. Their fitted charge parity, distinct reference branching and supplied gap/clock are not silently identified with the earlier branch-character rule or the count-selecting centered-window action.

13.3 Bridges That Remain Necessary

A bridge is a derived relation between two candidate descriptions: for example, a reduction showing that the components and conserved quantities of one action obey the equations used in another. Reusing the same letter, charge table or spatial dimension is not such a relation. The outstanding bridges below identify precisely what must connect the useful constructions.

The minimal real clock fibre and the full massive complex Clifford field are different hypotheses. Minimal active-fibre isolation might reconcile them, but it has not been derived. One cannot apply the selector to the large field while silently discarding its clock-restoring multiplicities.

The normal six-plane in the charge construction and the electron's bound six-plane are different subspaces. They coexist geometrically, but identifying them would change the construction. Likewise the pure pencil does not generate all intermediate bound directions, and preserving a fixed nested flag reduces literal normal rotation symmetry.

Spatial Hodge indices and independent color indices are different. Their joint current is explicit, but matching the integer three never suffices to identify their transformations. The fixed zero-order normal color commutant test also differs from total angular color that rotates coordinates; its depth restrictions cannot be transferred to the latter without checking.

The positive second-order localization action supplies different equations and canonical charges from the first-order Clifford construction. Its numerical profile has two phase velocities. No common reduction currently lets it inherit the first-order half-spin/charge proofs or the one-fundamental portion law. The problem is a missing bridge, not that the useful individual results are false.

Classical norms remain continuous. Relative charge weights, half-angle transformation and a mass-frequency label do not separately fix their absolute integrated source strengths. A common physical normalization is needed wherever spin, charge and inertia are compared quantitatively. Section 9.5 supplies a conditional amplitude-independent charge normalization using a finite same-field marginal, but leaves the common charge unit undetermined and does not normalize spin or inertia. Its nonlocal construction must still be connected to a physical response law. This curvature source is a different object from the norm-weighted charge ∫Ψ†QΨ\int\Psi^\dagger Q\Psi∫Ψ†QΨ; no relation between the two currents has been derived.

13.4 The Joint Evidential Claim

There are now several concrete overlaps, with distinct premises. One full-space radial preparation of a density action joins support, nonzero clock, positive calculated momentum response and polarization/current geometry. A separate centered-window action joins prepared spin and normal charge–color carriers, localization, controlled first-simplex weights and exact weak translating fields; its positive initial response is not a proved positive relaxed dispersion mass. Exact centered-only polynomial fields also retain spatially varying normal geometry and its full normal representation range. These are conditional analytical and numerical results, not independent experimental observations. The selected four-plus-six charge construction remains a different preparation. More broadly, useful geometric choices do more than one job, and some of their combinations have been calculated explicitly. The complete three-component channels occur at the two assigned quark depths. A single exterior-component construction gives both relative charge fractions and their color transformation types. Requiring spin and independent color to coexist restricts the clock while preserving it. These are concrete relations between outputs, rather than a list of separately attached particle labels. The scoped curvature construction extends this approach: the orientation data governing circulation also enter a spatial integral of the charge rule, with charge retained during specified shape changes. Its contribution is a bridge between descriptions, not another statistically independent charge match.

The shared assumptions are compatible at several demonstrated algebraic and source-action levels. There is no established single action realizing every row of the table at once. That is the present answer to the compatibility question; assuming complete compatibility would overstate it, while treating each successful calculation as isolated would understate it.

The interest is the intersection of restrictions. The mass comparisons provide a proposed organization to test. The minimal clock criterion reproduces its depth set under its own component premise; the finite spinor profile supports the assigned matter depths; the channel calculations distinguish the quark pair. Charge and polarization then supply further structure and compatibility checks. Some constructions select dimensions, while others establish relationships among properties without uniquely selecting their depths. Keeping those contributions distinct makes their combined value assessable.

Shared choices can reduce the number of independently supplied ingredients and expose additional ways for a model to fail. That is explanatory value. Establishing statistical independence or dependence of empirical tests is a separate task requiring a joint model; sharing a premise alone settles neither. Section 5.3 quantifies the joint numerical mass-and-ratio event under its explicit reference distribution and fixed prescription. Its conditional coverage is not a probability for the complete physical theory, and the geometric results are not multiplied into it as additional probability factors.

14. What the Programme Has Established and What Would Complete It

The exact mathematics includes the simplex identities, the conditional assignment certificates, full-profile spin covariance and norm integrals, minimal-module clock classification, complete middle-Hodge rank theorem, color contractions, the conditional two-plane polarization algebra, exterior charge weights, free differential charge conservation, conjugate map and the stated stress/response identities. Each has its hypotheses above. Numerical localization is supporting calculation under a declared action, with restricted stability and discretization limits, rather than an existence proof.

The suspected physical picture is a common field sustaining finite patterns of different spatial involvement, with a kind-specific fundamental and count-proportional registered frequency. The same geometry may control which patterns support half-spin, polarization structure, independent color and the relative charge blocks. Deterministic trajectories describe particle centres; internal oscillations and detector averages remain separate. Same-field response produces interactions without exchanged particles.

The first-order density results in sections 9.6–9.7 and 12.9–12.11 add an exact restricted geometric solution, positive-clock reduced charge branches, and a complete-space numerical candidate with positive momentum response and checked local circulation geometry. This materially reduces the gap between property algebra and spatial dynamics, without identifying all constructions with one physical particle. The conditional neutrino spectrum supplies an additional concrete observational target after one splitting calibration.

The compact-profile results in sections 12.6–12.8 add exact support, a finite restricted energy basin and a mechanical clock construction under explicit premises. They do not replace the geometric property proofs or establish that one field solution realizes all of them.

The central unfinished derivation is a common spatial dynamics that selects the occupied n, sustains C common-frequency portions, preserves the physical charge/color source under encounters, and matches the sector-scale prescription with consistent normalization. Required tests include the actual bound/free support, full 10+1 response, the neutral five-depth branch, equal charged-lepton electric response, finite-lived versus persistent branches, and full reciprocal energy/momentum balance. Resolving bottom, neutrino absolute scale and physical antipattern identification remains part of the programme. No completed mass operator or experimental confirmation is claimed.

For a collaborator, the immediate opportunity is to make one of the existing connections hold at the level of the governing equation. Three concrete routes are:

  1. Carry the clock selector into a sustained spatial field. Derive why the active components obey the minimal clock premise while retaining the spatial derivatives needed by the complete field. Then test whether that same law selects the occupied count and its fundamental.
  2. Preserve the charge and color constructions during interactions. Extend the checked isolated-field labels to a reciprocal equation, retaining the relative charge fractions, equal charged-lepton electric response and the depth-five neutral branch.
  3. Join support and inertia to the property geometry. Use the charge-preserving profiles of section 9.5 as concrete tests of supporting dynamics: derive a sustained core and exterior orientation tail, then test its clock, inertia and reciprocal response. The known static profile and the finite-radius trial are different constructions; a common equation must establish which successful features coexist.

These routes meet at the same test: does a common field law retain several successful results without separately adjusting each particle? The case for investigation rests on the reproducible relations already available, the geometric choices that produce several consequences together, and the explicit combinations that narrow this remaining task.

Appendix B. Explicit Matrix and Operator Recipes

B.1 Clifford Matrices and the Charge/Spin Calculation

This recipe turns the abstract Clifford relations into explicit small matrices. A tensor power means repeated tensor products; an exponent zero means that factor is absent. Each Pauli matrix has two rows and columns, so five factors give 25=322^5=3225=32 rows and columns. This is a component-matrix size, not a spatial dimension. The “occupation” numbers in this recipe label exterior degree algebraically, not counted physical particles.

Let X,Y,Z be the ordinary Pauli matrices and I the two-by-two identity. For q=0,...,4, construct

γ2q+1=Z⊗q⊗X⊗I⊗(4−q),γ2q+2=Z⊗q⊗Y⊗I⊗(4−q).(B.1) \gamma_{2q+1}=Z^{\otimes q}\otimes X\otimes I^{\otimes(4-q)},\quad \gamma_{2q+2}=Z^{\otimes q}\otimes Y\otimes I^{\otimes(4-q)}. \tag{B.1} γ2q+1​=Z⊗q⊗X⊗I⊗(4−q),γ2q+2​=Z⊗q⊗Y⊗I⊗(4−q).(B.1)

They are 32-by-32 Hermitian matrices. A normalized product proportional to all ten provides beta. For each normal pair define occupation na=(I−iγ2a+3γ2a+4)/2n_a=(I-i\gamma_{2a+3}\gamma_{2a+4})/2na​=(I−iγ2a+3​γ2a+4​)/2, a=1,2,3; thus the normal spin sum is ∑ana−3/2\sum_an_a-3/2∑a​na​−3/2. Project onto even total normal occupation j=0 or 2, form Gamma4 as in (10.2), and diagonalize (3Γ4/2+∑ana−3/2)/3(3\Gamma_4/2+\sum_an_a-3/2)/3(3Γ4​/2+∑a​na​−3/2)/3. The multiplicities must be 2 at -1, 6 at -1/3, 2 at 0 and 6 at 2/3. The matrices −iγ2γ3/2-i\gamma_2\gamma_3/2−iγ2​γ3​/2 and cyclic permutations have squared sum 3I/4 and commute with this restricted Q. These operations reproduce the lowest-angular charge/spin table without referring to a named particle.

To reproduce the differential identity rather than just its lowest matrix, apply D4X4+X4D4=2E4+4D_4X_4+X_4D_4=2E_4+4D4​X4​+X4​D4​=2E4​+4 to a smooth test spinor and use [E4,D4]=−D4[E_4,D_4]=-D_4[E4​,D4​]=−D4​. Substituting B4 from (10.2) gives B4D4+D4B4=0B_4D_4+D_4B_4=0B4​D4​+D4​B4​=0. Multiplication by the anticommuting Gamma4 then gives [K4,D4]=0[K_4,D_4]=0[K4​,D4​]=0. Normal gammas commute with Gamma4 and B4, while total normal rotations commute with the normal Dirac contraction. This proves the full free commutator, including every spatial derivative. Boundary conditions must still make integrated generators well-defined.

B.2 A Small Exact Way to Reproduce the Real Clock Table

The entries in the following words label real two-by-two matrix factors. Counting commutation signs lets the clock commutant be found without solving a large approximate linear system. “Bitwise XOR” is a discrete operation on the labels that records matrix multiplication up to a sign; the explicit skew and commutation rules retain the signs relevant to the test.

Real matrix words avoid a large symbolic nullspace. Use the real basis I,X,Z,AI,X,Z,AI,X,Z,A, with A=(0−110)A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)A=(01​−10​), labeled 0,1,2,3. Distinct nonidentity letters anticommute. Tensor words commute when the number of positions containing distinct nonidentity letters is even; they are skew exactly when they contain an odd number of A letters. Product labels are bitwise XOR, up to an irrelevant sign.

For the quaternionic four-real-component module use generator words (3,0), (2,3), (1,3). Seven mutually anticommuting real eight-by-eight negative-square generators are

(3,0,0), (2,3,0), (2,2,3), (2,1,3),
(1,0,3), (1,3,1), (1,3,2).

Spin(5), Spin(6) and Spin(7) use pair products from their first five, six and seven generators. A chiral Spin(8) uses all seven and their pair products. For Spin(9), prepend A to each of the seven and append X tensor I8 and Z tensor I8, obtaining nine positive-square generators on R16; their pair products generate rotations. For Spin(10), prepend Z to those nine and append X tensor I16, then take pair products on R32. Enumerating all words commuting with these rotations and counting the skew ones gives the table in section 7. Spin(2) uses A, and Spin(1) is scalar. This is an exact finite computation of the minimal-module commutants. It does not justify minimality as a physical premise.

B.3 Hodge, Color and the Joint Clock Check

An increasing index subset chooses an oriented basis blade. The complementary subset supplies the Hodge partner, and the permutation sign records their orientation. In the color recipe, EijE_{ij}Eij​ is the matrix with one in row iii, column jjj, and zeros elsewhere. A Gram matrix collects inner products between the commutator matrices; its diagonal form records the squared failure of each clock direction to commute with color, including the zero mixed terms.

Enumerate increasing m-index subsets I of {1,...,2m}. The star matrix maps each basis blade to its complementary blade with the sign of the permutation (I,I-complement). Squaring it gives (-1) to the m times I; its transpose has the same parity sign. Half its dimension is the rank in (8.3). The construction uses physical Euclidean spatial forms only.

For an explicit normalized color basis take, for each i<j, (Eij+Eji)/2(E_{ij}+E_{ji})/2(Eij​+Eji​)/2 and (−iEij+iEji)/2(-iE_{ij}+iE_{ji})/2(−iEij​+iEji​)/2, and the two diagonals diag(1,-1,0)/2 and diag(1,1,-2)/(2 sqrt(3)). These eight Hermitian matrices reproduce (8.5) entry by entry. Tensoring them with the identity on the spin doublet and converting a complex matrix M into (Re⁡M−Im⁡MIm⁡MRe⁡M)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\operatorname{Re}M&-\operatorname{Im}M\\ \operatorname{Im}M&\operatorname{Re}M\end{smallmatrix}\right)(ReMImM​−ImMReM​) gives the real twelve-by-twelve color action. Complex conjugation is diag(I6,-I6). Construct J0,J1,J2 as in section 7 and sum their commutator Gram matrix. It is diag(0,10/3,10/3), proving (7.5), including the absence of mixed terms.

B.4 Running and Retrieving the Evidence

Download the finite-calculation program and save it as particle-geometry-checks.py. Python with NumPy and SymPy is sufficient. Running

python particle-geometry-checks.py

writes particle-geometry-checks.json beside the program and prints its pass status and executed source hash. The joint mass-and-ratio appendix separately provides its complete input data and two programs. The clock-connectivity proposal has its own checker and explicitly different review status.

The displayed equations and recipes are sufficient to reproduce the finite comparisons without access to the private research catalog. The large localization solve is specified by its action, measure, boundary prescription and convergence tests; the small checker does not rerun it.

The scalar, clock, Hodge and color tests in this program are finite identities. Numerical matrix comparisons check the finite instances to the stated tolerance, with the general proofs given in the text. They are not tests of actual particle trajectories, a physical field amplitude, full nonlinear stability or agreement with every experimental observable.

Appendix C. Combined Glossary and Index

This appendix defines terms and symbols and points to their first substantial explanation or calculation. The section links are the locators; no page numbers are assumed. A symbol can have several meanings in different candidate constructions. Those meanings are listed explicitly rather than being silently identified. All component and representation language describes the one field on ordinary physical 10+1 spacetime.

Inertia, complete Response of the complete localized solution's energy and momentum under motion, including its supporting stress. 12.5
Inner product; norm Component overlap and magnitude, locally or integrated over space. Their mathematical use introduces no Born probability law. 2.2; 6.3
Integrated color neutrality Vanishing of all integrated traceless color charges. It need not hold pointwise in the density. 12.2
Invariant Unchanged under the transformations specified in the claim. The transformation group and whether parameters are global must be named. 7.1; 8.2; 12.1
Irreducible/minimal representation A representation with no smaller invariant decomposition / the specified smallest spinor carrier. Multiplicity or a larger carrier can change the conclusions. 7.1; 7.3
Isometry A map preserving the stated inner product or squared norm. The odd-shadow map needs its 1/21/\sqrt21/2​ normalization. 8.1
Isotropic annihilator Complex-encoded directions with zero bilinear quadratic form whose Clifford action annihilates a spinor. It does not make real Euclidean directions null. 9.2; 9.3
Kernel; rank Inputs mapped to zero / number of independent outputs. A rank theorem depends on which complete map and carrier were specified. 2.2; 7.2; 8.1
Kinetic term/order Derivative part of the action or equation. First- and second-order candidate dynamics have different canonical structures. 7.1; 10.1; 12.1
Laue condition Vanishing integrated spatial stress under the stated localization, conservation and stationary-rest-stress hypotheses. 12.5
Linear response The first-order response around a specified configuration. It does not establish arbitrary-amplitude stability. 12.4
Localization; support Concentration near a spatial region / the region where a field is nonzero. Decaying tails may have infinite support but finite norm or energy. 6.3; 12.2
Lorentz boost/scalar A transformation between uniformly moving spacetime frames / a component with the stated scalar transformation law. The latter is an extra premise of section 12. 12.1; 12.5
Magnetic moment; ggg diagnostic A moment of current / its specified dimensionless ratio to charge and spin using the comparison coupling. It is not yet an IDWT electron prediction. 11.3
Mass state versus flavor A state labeled by a mass eigenvalue versus an interaction label. The neutrino count test uses mass states. 4.2
Middle form Degree mmm in 2m2m2m directions, so its Hodge complement has the same degree. 8.1
Monomial; degree A product of coordinate powers / their summed exponent. These label the cumulative count. 3.1
Multiplicity Number of repeated representation copies or eigenvectors sharing an eigenvalue. Repeated real-type copies can restore a clock. 2.2; 7.2; 7.3
Noether charge Integrated current associated with a continuous action symmetry, conserved on solutions if boundary flux vanishes. 12.1
Normal direction An ordinary spatial direction perpendicular to a specified subspace. “Normal six” is not automatically the electron's bound six. 8.2; 9.3
Normalization Specifying a component norm, kinetic coefficient or physical source scale. These are different operations and must not be conflated. 4.1; 9.1; 12.1
Operator A rule acting on components or fields. Differential operators also act on their spatial dependence. 2.2; 10.1
Orbital contribution Coordinate-dependent part of a spatial field rotation generator. Here it is not the electron's external orbit around a nucleus. 9.4; 11.2
Parity Even/odd exterior degree, or a specified spatial reflection symmetry according to context. These uses are distinguished in their calculations. 8.2; 8.3; 11.1
Pauli matrices Three Hermitian two-by-two matrices used for spin and tensor-product recipes. Repeated copies act on distinct algebraic factors. 6.4; 9.4; B.1
Phase; phase locking Position in an oscillation cycle / fixed relative phases at a common frequency. Locking need not make all portions reach a crest simultaneously. 3.3
Phase action A canonical quantity associated with a component phase. In the interacting action only the stated symmetry combinations are conserved; the individual contributions need not be. These quantities need not be integers. 12.1; 12.2
Norm current The current associated with conserved squared field magnitude in a specified evolution equation. It is not automatically electric current, energy flux or centre motion. 6.6
Polarization For light, the directions, relative magnitudes and phases of two transverse components; for matter, spin orientation. Higher-depth spatial textures and their relation to these observables are investigated separately. 6.4; 6.5; 6.6
Positive-energy projection Retention of the positive free-energy branch. It changes the norm measure and need not require a positive-β\betaβ seed. 11.3
Positive completion Squared norm of a component mismatch that supplies both coupling and its square terms. Positivity alone is not full stability. 11.5; 12.1
Projector An operation satisfying P2=PP^2=PP2=P, selecting a component subspace. Dynamical closure under the full equation needs a separate check. 2.2; 8.2; 9.3
Projected norm measure Fourier weight including the positive-energy factor (1+sM/Ep)/2(1+sM/E_p)/2(1+sM/Ep​)/2, normalized by NsN_sNs​. 11.3
Pullback; contraction Restricting a form to a subspace / inserting a vector to remove one form index. A four-form must be contracted before the stated three-dimensional restriction. 8.3
Pure spinor/pencil A spinor with maximal isotropic annihilator / a two-dimensional family all of whose nonzero members are pure. 9.2; 9.3
Quartic/sextic potential Terms of degree four/six in field amplitudes, such as ρ2,ρ3\rho^2,\rho^3ρ2,ρ3. Their signs control the stated focusing and defocusing contributions. 12.1
Quaternionic type A real representation with quaternion algebra in its commutant, providing three imaginary skew directions. 7.1
Quiet sector The exact second-order ansatz with zero singlets and retained triplet texture. “Quiet” does not mean that the triplet phases stop evolving. 12.2
Reciprocal interaction Both patterns respond through the same action, including field backreaction, rather than one being a prescribed receiver. 10.2; 12.1
Relative equilibrium A configuration stationary in shape while component phases advance at their specified rates. The numerical quiet core has two such rates. 12.2
Representation A rule assigning matrices or operators to transformations while preserving how those transformations compose. 6.1; 7.4
Residual; convergence Equation mismatch for a computed profile / evidence that refinement approaches the continuum problem. A discrete small residual is not a continuum existence proof. 12.2
Routh functional Energy minus phase frequencies times conserved actions, used for the fixed-frequency stationary and relaxation tests. 12.3
Sector A classification of pattern depth or a preserved solution ansatz, as stated locally. It is not an additional physical manifold. 3.2; 12.2
Seed Constant component data from which an explicit spatial profile is constructed. Its spin and β\betaβ signs do not by themselves fix complete physical observables. 6.1; 11.2
Shadow The specified odd-dimensional form channel induced from its containing even-dimensional spatial construction. It is an additional premise. 8.1
Simplex Higher-dimensional generalization of a segment, triangle or tetrahedron. The count uses a simplex in exponent labels without proving the particle's physical shape. 3.1
Skew; nondegenerate A real matrix with JT=−JJ^T=-JJT=−J / an invertible pairing with no unpaired nonzero direction. 7.1
Source law The physical rule relating field data and conserved current to reciprocal response. A charge-weight table alone does not supply it. 8.3; 10.2
Spatial band All chosen spatial polynomial labels through a degree cutoff, combined with component data and a decaying envelope. 7.2
Spin; spinor; Spin(d) Rotation behavior / components carrying a spin representation / the double cover of spatial rotations retaining the spinor sign. 6.1; 6.2
Stabilizer Transformations leaving specified data fixed. Preserving a spatial flag can reduce the available normal group. 9.3
Stability Persistence against specified perturbations. Restricted Hessian positivity, binding, nonlinear stability and observed lifetime are different claims. 12.2; 12.3
Stationarity Vanishing first variation under allowed changes, or a time-independent shape under specified phase motion. It is not synonymous with full stability. 6.1; 11.4; 12.2
Stress Directional momentum flow and internal forces. Complete balance is required for the conditional localized inertia result. 11.4; 12.5
SU(2), SU(3), U(3), SO(d) Groups of determinant-one unitary two-/three-component operations, general unitary three-component operations, and real orientation-preserving spatial rotations, respectively. They specify operations, not the topology of spacetime. 6.1; 7.4; 8.2
Symmetry versus topology Symmetry concerns transformations preserving specified data or laws. Topology concerns global connectedness and holes. A group label does not establish a spatial topology. 7.4
Tensor product/direct sum Simultaneous pairs of component labels / alternative component blocks. Neither automatically supplies new physical degrees of freedom. 2.2; 9.1
Transverse/longitudinal Perpendicular/parallel to a stated direction or momentum. The reference direction must be specified. 6.4; 12.4
Virial identity Necessary balance obtained by a scale variation of a stationary constrained functional. It is not by itself an existence theorem. 11.4; 12.5
Weight Phase exponent or generator eigenvalue under a stated one-parameter transformation. 9.1
Wedge product Antisymmetric product of oriented form components; repeated directions give zero. 8.1; 8.3
Zero mode A profile in the kernel of a specified operator. A zero normal eigenvalue does not establish zero complete particle mass. 9.4
Compact profile and finite basin An exact supported shape and a nonlinear energy bound within a fixed-ball relative-profile class; not a dynamical invariance theorem. 12.6
Source-affine clock A rest Hamiltonian with derivative Omega with respect to each independent phase action. It preserves the common fundamental in the stated canonical chart. 12.7
Connectivity Laplacian A finite matrix of spatial coupling weights; rank C−K counts independent connections for K components. It is not another physical space. 12.7
Prescribed-probe susceptibility A controlled first shape response to an imposed gradient, before deriving a reciprocal particle-pair law. 12.8

Complete-space density candidate. The first-order trial law and radial preparation of sections 12.9–12.11, depending on every physical spatial coordinate. Finite approximate support is distinguished from exact nonlinear existence.

Horizontal derivative. The part of a component's spatial derivative perpendicular to its own ray; equation (9.16). It removes magnitude/common-phase derivatives for a geometric diagnostic, not for the full physical kinetic equation.

Momentum response. The derivative of conserved momentum with respect to a putative whole-pattern velocity; equations (12.27)–(12.29). A tangent calculation is not a proved finite-velocity family.

Local circulation plane. The real plane extracted from complete spinor bilinears by (12.31), where its denominator is nonzero. Its norm-current curves are distinct from a particle-centre trajectory and temporal clock.

C.3 Questions and evidence locators

If the question is… Start here
What does the exact count prove, and what remains physical? 3.1–3.3
Which numbers were prescribed or calibrated? 4.1–4.3, including both separate neutrino benchmarks
How strong is the alternative-depth test? 5.1 for the fixed-index diagnostic; 5.2 for the conditional unrestricted-index theorem
Why does the spatial pattern have half-spin? 6.1–6.3; distinguish its seed premise, full rotation law and continuous norm
How do two photon polarization components connect to depth, and how might matter generalize this? 6.4; 6.5, with observed spin projections distinguished from spatial depth
Which component-carrier assumptions select depths? 7.1–7.3; 8.4
Does “three channels” already derive SU(3) color? 8.1–8.3; the answer requires the separate transformation and source assumptions
What does the relative-charge table establish? 9.1, then 10.1–10.2 for kinetic and interaction tests
Are the selected normal six directions the electron's six bound directions? 9.3
What is actually established at depth five? 9.4, including the distinct generator, texture and bubble assumptions
Is the magnetic moment a particle prediction? 11.3; the source coupling, preparation and normalization remain conditional
What did the localization numerics solve? 12.1–12.2, with the exact action, ten-space measure and grid table
What fails outside the quiet ansatz, and what repairs it? 12.3; the repair is scoped to the stated singlet escape and fixed-shape bounds
Are response tails mediator particles? 12.4; they solve an equation for an already retained field component
When is complete positive inertia established conditionally? 12.5, including stationary rest stress and boundary assumptions
Do all results belong to one established particle theory? 13.1–13.4, especially the carrier/action distinctions
Where are the exact sources, programs and reproduction rules? Appendix A; Appendix B
